9.1 — Binary: How Numbers Live in Memory

All semester you have typed int and float like they were words. Underneath, every one of your coins, every xSpeed of 5, every cooldown of 2f is a stack of bits — and once you can READ them, half the AP exam's data questions become easy points.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I read a number as bits?”
Break It Down~10 min

Read the number 13 as eight bits of memory — and be able to say what every single bit is worth.

First, before anything else: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Name the place valueswhat does this part do?Read: the place-value table in this lesson, in the Concept Lab
  2. Walk the places from largest to smallestwhat does this part do?Read: Step 2 of the Build Lab below
  3. Say why the hardware counts in twos and not tenswhat does this part do?Read: Binary & Hex, the unit reference page
  4. Work out how far a fixed width can reachwhat does this part do?Read: the byte-vs-int range discussion in the Concept Lab
  5. Recognise the edgewhat does this part do?Read: the overflow practice on the Exam Reference Sheet

The split is the whole lesson. "Convert 13 to binary" is one task you can only memorise; these five are five things you can look up, and the last two are the ones the exam actually asks about. Nothing here needs a variable — a bit width is a *design* decision you make once, and every later bug in this unit is that decision meeting a number that grew past it.

The test: could you explain this part to somebody using only a piece of paper? If a part needs Unity open to explain, it is not a part of this problem — it is a part of a coding problem.

Connect it to something you already know

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

You want to store the number of lessons in the year, 81. Does it fit in 7 bits? Name the power of two that decides it, and say what that tells you about picking a width.

Unity spends a whole byte on a bool even though a bool is one bit. Is that waste a mistake? Argue one sentence for each side.

In 2.1 your coin count was an int that only ever went up. Now that you know an int is 32 bits wide, that counter has a ceiling nobody chose out loud — what is it, and what happens one step past it?

In 2.3 you put a cap on health so it could not climb forever. A bit width is the same idea, imposed by hardware instead of by you. Which of those two caps can you change, and which one can you not?

In 4.1, direction = direction * -1 reversed your enemy. In binary, negation is a pattern operation on the bits rather than arithmetic on the number. Which of the two explanations is the real one?

Concept Lab ~15 min

Base 10 first (you already know it). The number 273 means 2×100 + 7×10 + 3×1. Each place is worth TEN times the one to its right, because you have ten fingers' worth of symbols (0–9). Binary is the same game with two symbols:

Place8s4s2s1s
Bits1011
Worth8021

1011₂ = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Each place is a power of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.

Why computers chose 2. Every wire in the machine holds either HIGH or LOW, on or off, 1 or 0 — your game runs on billions of yes/no questions per second. An 8-bit number (a byte) counts 0–255; an int like your health (3) or coins (0) is 32 bits wide, so its range is enormous — but NOT infinite, and that is the fact that matters:

Your turret cooldown 2f stored as a float:
0 10000000 00000000000000000000000  → the bits of 2.0f
(int) 2f is 00000000000000000000000000000010  → the bits of 2

Socratic

Coins are an int, maxHealth is an int, jumpForce is a float. Why would coins NEVER want to be a float — and what goes wrong with money (0.1 + 0.2) in binary? Try it: Debug.Log(0.1f + 0.2f == 0.3f); — why does it print False?

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — count in binary with your hands. Right thumb = 1, right index = 2, right middle = 4, right ring = 8, right pinky = 16. Count 0–31 by raising fingers. When you can get to your coin count without stalls, you have it.

Step 2 — read your own game's numbers. Convert, on paper, into 8-bit binary:

  1. health = 3 → 00000011
  2. attackCooldown = 2 → 00000010
  3. maxAttackRange = 7 → 00000111
  4. patrolDistance = 3, chaseDistance = 5 → convert both
  5. The number of B days in the semester: 81 lessons → does it fit in 7 bits? (128 says yes, 64 says no — which one is right?)

Step 3 — bit tricks your game ALREADY plays. direction = direction * -1 from 4.1? In binary, negation is a bit pattern operation (two's complement: flip every bit, add 1). And your booleans — hasAxe, isGrounded, isOnLadder — are single bits. A byte could hold EIGHT of your booleans. Unity spends a byte per bool anyway — memory is cheap now, but the exam wants you to KNOW a bool is a bit.

Bug Hunt: Bit logic

  1. What is the largest 4-bit number? (1111₂ = 15 — why is "all ones" always one less than the next power?)
  2. 10000000₂ + 10000000₂ = ? (Warning: in 8 bits, the answer OVERFLOWS. What happens to the ninth bit — and what does your int do when it overflows?)
  3. Write int max = int.MaxValue; then Debug.Log(max + 1); — run it. What number printed, and why is the biggest positive suddenly the most negative? Then try the one-liner int.MaxValue + 1: it will not even compile. Why does the compiler refuse arithmetic the running program does without complaint?
  4. Your coins count past 2,147,483,647 (impossible on foot — but a cheat could). What is the smallest code change that prevents the overflow?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Own it

  1. Write your birth year in binary. (Check with a partner — each digit of YOUR answer should be verifiable by powers of two.)
  2. AP practice: "A video game stores a player's health as an 8-bit binary number. What is the maximum health?" — write the answer and the REASON (2⁸ − 1), not just the number.
  3. Hard: one bit of extra health (a 9th bit) doubles the max. Why does +1 bit mean ×2 range — and why do we not just add bits forever (what is the tradeoff the exam keeps asking about)?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Convert any small decimal to binary and back, showing powers of two
  • Explain WHY hardware uses base 2 (voltage states)
  • Demonstrate int overflow and explain it with bits
  • Say what a bool really costs and why range doubles per bit
